question: A 25-year-old woman sustains a high-energy open tibial fracture after a road traffic accident. There is a large, contaminated wound >10 cm, exposed bone, and absent popliteal pulse requiring vascular surgery. What is the correct Gustilo-Anderson grade?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IIIA has adequate soft-tissue coverage despite the large wound. The absent pulse requiring vascular repair immediately upgrades this to IIIC.
IIIB has extensive soft-tissue loss requiring flap coverage but an intact vascular supply. Absent pulse needing repair = IIIC.
Correct. IIIC is defined by an arterial injury requiring vascular repair, regardless of the wound size or contamination level. This carries the highest amputation risk (up to 50% at 6 months).
Grade II wounds are >1 cm but with minimal contamination and adequate soft-tissue coverage. A vascular injury alone mandates Grade III classification.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key differentiator: if there is an arterial injury requiring vascular repair, it is Grade IIIC regardless of wound size or contamination.
Correct. IIIC = arterial injury requiring repair. Memorise: IIIA = coverage adequate, IIIB = flap required, IIIC = artery cut.
